entries.title: NOAA NCEI global climate monitoring
entries.summary: NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) tracks global surface, land, and ocean temperature anomalies since 1850 alongside Northern Hemisphere snow cover, Arctic and Antarctic sea ice extent, and global tropical cyclone counts.

entries.title: Earthquakes and tectonic plate faults
entries.summary: Per USGS, earthquakes occur when tectonic plate stress overcomes friction in a sudden fault slip, radiating seismic waves through the crust. Larger mainshocks are followed by readjustment aftershocks along the fault zone that decrease in frequency over time.

entries.title: Earth's ocean area and water distribution
entries.summary: Per NOAA and USGS, the ocean covers over 70 percent of Earth's surface and holds about 97 percent of Earth's water—roughly 1,335,000,000 cubic kilometers of 1,386,000,000 cubic kilometers total—while about 2 percent is frozen in glaciers and ice caps and under 1 percent is fresh.

entries.title: NASA Earth observations and USGS Land Cover (NLCD)
entries.summary: NASA Earth Observatory and NASA POWER publish global satellite observations of Earth systems and solar parameters, while the USGS National Land Cover Database (NLCD) maps conterminous U.S. land cover and urban imperviousness at 30-meter resolution across 2001-2021 epochs.

entries.title: Volcanoes, earthquakes and disasters

tiers.everyday: Famous eruptions and earthquakes on the globe, from Vesuvius in 79 CE to Mount St. Helens in 1980. Each pin is the official published point from NOAA, and every number names its source.
tiers.student: A curated first batch from the NOAA NCEI Significant Volcanic Eruptions and Significant Earthquake databases (doi:10.7289/V5JW8BSH, doi:10.7289/V5TD9V7K), with USGS pages for context. Where NCEI and USGS give different death tolls, both are shown. Pins are NCEI's published points, so they are approximate.

entries.title: Krakatau eruption, 1883

tiers.everyday: In August 1883 the Krakatau volcano in Indonesia blew apart. The explosions were heard about 5,000 km away, and the tsunami that followed killed tens of thousands of people.
tiers.student: NOAA NCEI lists the 27 August 1883 eruption of Krakatau at VEI 6, with 36,417 deaths in total. USGS gives about 36,000 and names the tsunami as the main cause. A USGS Volcano Watch article says about 25 km³ of material was thrown out, the island nearly vanished, and dust in the stratosphere lowered global temperatures.

entries.title: Tambora eruption, 1815

tiers.everyday: In April 1815 Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted. Tens of thousands of people died, many of them later from hunger, and USGS says its effect on the atmosphere was probably bigger than that of Pinatubo in 1991.
tiers.student: NOAA NCEI rates the eruption of 10 April 1815 at VEI 7, the highest in this batch, and counts 11,000 direct deaths and 60,000 in total. The USGS deadliest-eruptions table gives 92,000, mainly from starvation. The two totals disagree, so both are shown.

entries.title: Lisbon earthquake and tsunami, 1755

tiers.everyday: On 1 November 1755 a great earthquake struck under the Atlantic off Portugal. A study listed by USGS describes it as the most destructive quake Europe has known, and its tsunami reached coasts on both sides of the ocean.
tiers.student: NOAA NCEI lists magnitude 8.5 (Mw), intensity XI on the Modified Mercalli scale and 50,000 deaths, and links a tsunami. A 2009 study estimated Mw 8.5–9.0 and put the tsunami at about 5–15 m on the shores of Portugal and Morocco, with accounts from Caribbean islands, Brazil and Newfoundland. Where the fault lies is still debated.
